title: Data Sources
text: Data Sources Collected firsthand by the researcher for a specific research purpose Collected through surveys, experiments, interviews, or direct observations More control and specificity but can be expensive and time-consuming Primary Data Has already been collected by someone else and is available for use by researchers Existing databases, official reports, published studies, and archival records More accessible and cost- effective but may not be tailored to the exact needs of the research Secondary Data

title: Quality concerns when using secondary data
text: Quality concerns when using secondary data Concerns Consequences Mitigations Missing values Biased results if not properly handled. The extent and pattern of missing data (random or systematic) also affect the validity of the analysis. Imputation, deletion of missing cases, or using methods like maximum likelihood estimation Outliers Distortion of patterns, especially in small datasets Removal (be careful! Some are legitimate) Sensitivity analysis to determine influence. Measurement errors Caused by inconsistencies in data collection methods, coding errors, or changes in definitions over time. Inaccurate results. Cross-validate with other sources. Apply correction techniques if the error structure is known. Representative ness Over- or under-sampling of certain groups or lack sufficient geographic or demographic coverage. Weightings. Carefully interpreting and generalizing findings.

title: Statistical software packages
text: Statistical software packages Available for free for CAM students Pros and Cons Best at … Excel Great for basic analysis and data manipulation, but limited for advanced quantitative analysis. Up to 16 independent variables in regression analysis. Checking outliers and missing values Preliminary analysis (charts and tables) Descriptive statistics Visualisation of results SPSS User-friendly and ideal for social sciences, but limited in flexibility and advanced methods. https://cambridge.store.academia.co.uk/ Standard regression analysis Not very good at time series analysis GUI, not much coding options STATA Excellent for econometrics and handling large datasets, but costly and not as flexible as R for customization. https://www.it.econ.cam.ac.uk/stata Standard and advanced regression analysis and time series analysis Write your own codes Run models/analyses in batches R Highly flexible, powerful, and open-source, but requires programming knowledge and has a steeper learning curve. https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/ Write your own codes Run models/analyses in batches Visualisation Advanced and new methods (ML, LLM, …)

title: Exercise 1: Inflation and REITs returns
text: Exercise 1: Inflation and REITs returns Instructions: Work in groups of two to complete the following tasks 1. Identify the data sources of the key variables – Anxious Index, realised and expected CPI inflation rates, and REITs returns in Connolly and Stivers (2024). 2. Download the Anxious Index (AI) and Median CPI Inflation Rate (CPI) from the Survey of Professional Forecasters (SPF) website. 3. Open the downloaded Excel files. Observe the data. Note any missing values or outliers. Find the variable definitions in each file (Hint: Documentations). 4. Determine the type of the data - are these cross-sectional, time series, or panel data? 5. Identify the statistical methods used in in Connolly and Stivers (2024). 6. Use a software package of your choice, generate descriptive statistics for the downloaded variables. 7. Use a software package of your choice, visualise the trends of Anxious Index and Expected Inflation Rate. 8. If you want to replicate this analysis by using data from the UK, can you find the corresponding data sources from the CRERC Databook? Discuss. 9. To estimate the model on page 929, which of the four software packages introduced in this lecture could be used? Discuss.

title: Exercise 2: Shrinking Homes in London
text: Exercise 2: Shrinking Homes in London Instructions: Work in groups of two to complete the following tasks 1. Identify the data sources of the key variables – property size from EPC and property transaction records in Hubbard et al, (2024). 2. Download the EPC data from the Department of Levelling up, Housing & Community’s website. 3. Download the property transaction data from the HM Land Registry Open Data website. 4. Open the downloaded files in Excel. Observe the data. Note any missing values or outliers. Find the variable definitions in each file (Hint: Documentations). 5. Determine the type of the data - are these cross-sectional, time series, or panel data? 6. Use a software package of your choice, generate descriptive statistics of the variables in the two datasets. 7. Use a software package of your choice, visualise the distribution of house prices (i.e., histograms or pie charts) in London. 8. If you want to replicate this study by using data from Cambridge, can you find the data to support your analysis? Discuss.
